title: “OUR GOD IS A CONSUMING FIRE” — THE TERRIFYING TRUTH ABOUT GOD THAT COULD BECOME THE MOST BEAUTIFUL THING YOU EVER UNDERSTAND
paragraphs: “OUR GOD IS A CONSUMING FIRE” — THE TERRIFYING TRUTH ABOUT GOD THAT COULD BECOME THE MOST BEAUTIFUL THING YOU EVER UNDERSTAND

What if the fire you have spent your life running from is the very fire that exposes your sin, destroys your false security, and calls you into the holiness, mercy, and unshakable love of Jesus Christ? Hebrews 12:29 is not merely a warning about judgment. It is an invitation to understand why grace should never be taken lightly.
There is something about fire that makes a human being stop.
You can ignore a whisper. You can walk past a warning sign. You can silence an alarm long enough to convince yourself that everything is fine.
But when flames begin climbing the walls, when smoke fills the room, when the heat reaches your skin, suddenly everything you thought was important becomes painfully insignificant.
The expensive furniture doesn't matter anymore.
The reputation you worked so hard to protect doesn't matter.
The possessions you spent years accumulating don't matter.
You just want to live.
Now imagine discovering that the Bible describes the God who created you, knows every secret you have ever buried, and holds your eternity in His hands with these breathtaking words:
“For our God is a consuming fire.” — Hebrews 12:29 (KJV)
Not a comforting candle.
Not a harmless flame you can control.
A consuming fire.
If God is a consuming fire, how can sinful people like us ever come near Him and survive?
Because the answer is not simply that God is dangerous.
The answer leads us straight to the cross of Jesus Christ.
And once you understand what Hebrews is actually saying, you may never look at God's holiness, your hidden sins, or the grace that saved you the same way again.
Perhaps the most frightening thing about standing before a holy God is not that He knows the worst thing you have ever done.
It is that He knows everything.
The thoughts you never spoke.
The bitterness you disguised as maturity.
The jealousy you called concern.
The lust you justified because nobody saw it.
The unforgiveness you carried while singing worship songs about mercy.
The quiet compromises that slowly became habits.
The version of yourself you carefully present to the world, and the version that appears when nobody is watching.
He sees both.
And still, through Jesus Christ, He calls sinners to repent, believe, and draw near.
That is where this story begins.
Not with a God who has lowered His standards to accommodate our rebellion.
But with a God so holy that sin cannot be treated as harmless, and so merciful that He gave His Son to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
To understand the fire, we must first understand the mountain.
Long before the writer of Hebrews declared that our God is a consuming fire, the people of Israel stood at the foot of Mount Sinai.
They had witnessed extraordinary deliverance.
God had brought them out of Egypt, broken the power of their oppressors, and led them through the sea.
They knew what it meant to be rescued.
But now they were about to discover something that modern Christianity sometimes forgets.
The God who delivers His people is also the God before whom His people must tremble.
Exodus 19 describes thunder, lightning, a thick cloud, and the terrifying sound of a trumpet.
The mountain shook.
Smoke rose.
The people trembled.
Why?
Because the LORD had descended upon Mount Sinai in fire.
Exodus 19:18 says:
“And mount Sinai was altogether on a smoke, because the LORD descended upon it in fire: and the smoke thereof ascended as the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mount quaked greatly.” (KJV)
Try to imagine standing there.
You have just been rescued from slavery.
You have seen the waters divide.
You have witnessed miracles that generations will remember.
And suddenly you realize that the God who saved you is not someone you can manipulate, domesticate, or approach on your own terms.
His presence is glorious.
His holiness is overwhelming.
His authority is absolute.
The mountain itself trembles.
And the people are afraid.
But do not miss what is happening.
God is not revealing His holiness because He enjoys frightening people.
He is revealing who He truly is.
He is teaching a redeemed people that belonging to Him is not permission to treat Him casually.
And that truth matters today.
Because somewhere along the way, many of us have become comfortable speaking about God as though He were merely an invisible companion whose primary responsibility is to approve our decisions.
We want His blessings without His commands.
His protection without His correction.
His promises without His holiness.
His forgiveness without repentance.
We want a Savior who rescues us from consequences, but sometimes resist the Lord who calls us to surrender.
And then Hebrews interrupts our comfortable assumptions.
“For our God is a consuming fire.”
The original Greek is just as striking.
καὶ γὰρ ὁ θεὸς ἡμῶν πῦρ καταναλίσκον.
Kai gar ho theos hēmōn pyr katanaliskon.
A close translation is:
“For indeed our God is a consuming fire.”
The word πῦρ (pyr) means “fire.”
The word καταναλίσκον (katanaliskon) is a present active participle from a verb meaning “to consume completely” or “use up.”
This is not a picture of a decorative flame.
It is a description of God's overwhelming holiness expressed through the biblical imagery of consuming fire.
But here is something crucial.
The writer of Hebrews did not invent this language.
He was drawing directly from Deuteronomy 4:24.
In the Hebrew Scriptures, we read:
כִּי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ אֵשׁ אֹכְלָה הוּא אֵל קַנָּא
Ki Adonai Elohekha esh okhlah hu, El qanna.
A close translation is:
“For the LORD your God is a consuming fire, a jealous God.”
The Hebrew expression אֵשׁ אֹכְלָה (esh okhlah) means “a consuming fire.”
And the word קַנָּא (qanna) describes God's jealousy in the context of His covenant relationship with His people.
Not the petty jealousy of an insecure human being.
Not the selfish possessiveness of someone terrified of losing control.
God's jealousy is His righteous insistence that His people must not abandon Him for idols.
He alone is God.
He alone is worthy of worship.
He will not pretend that false gods can save the people He has redeemed.
This is why the original context matters.
Deuteronomy 4 warns Israel against idolatry.
The consuming fire is not merely an illustration of emotional intensity.
It is a warning about the holiness of the covenant-making God and the seriousness of turning away from Him.
And Hebrews brings that same warning into the lives of people who have heard the Gospel.
Why?
Because grace does not make holiness irrelevant.
Grace brings us into a relationship with the Holy One.
Now we arrive at something that could change how you read Hebrews forever.
The words “our God is a consuming fire” do not appear in isolation.
They come at the end of one of the most magnificent passages about the privilege of belonging to Jesus Christ.
Hebrews 12 contrasts two mountains.
One is Sinai.
The mountain of trembling, darkness, and terrifying revelation.
The other is Mount Zion.
The heavenly Jerusalem.
The city of the living God.
The gathering of God's redeemed people.
And at the center of that astonishing picture stands Jesus.
Hebrews 12:24 calls Him:
“And to Jesus the mediator of the new covenant, and to the blood of sprinkling, that speaketh better things than that of Abel.” (KJV)
Read that again.
Jesus, the mediator of the new covenant.
The writer is not saying that the God of the Old Testament was terrifying while the God of the New Testament became harmless.
He is showing us that the same holy God has provided a better covenant through His Son.
The difference is not that God stopped being holy.
The difference is that Jesus has opened the way for sinners to approach God through His blood.
And this should leave us speechless.
Because the One whose holiness made Sinai tremble is the same God who welcomes redeemed sinners through Christ.
The God before whom the mountain shook has not changed.
But through Jesus, those who once stood condemned can receive mercy, forgiveness, and access to the Father.
That is not cheap grace.
That is astonishing grace.
And it cost more than any human being could ever pay.
Think about the cross for a moment.
Not the polished cross hanging on a wall.
Not the beautiful symbol printed on a shirt.
The actual cross.
The betrayal.
The false accusations.
The crown of thorns.
The humiliation.
The nails.
The suffering.
The darkness.
The Son of God giving His life for sinners.
The cross tells us something we desperately need to remember.
God does not overlook evil as though it were insignificant.
And God does not leave repentant sinners without hope.
At Calvary, divine justice and divine mercy are displayed in a way that should humble every human heart.
Romans 3:25–26 teaches that God presented Christ as the sacrifice through whom His righteousness is demonstrated, so that He is both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus.
That means God did not simply decide that sin no longer mattered.
Christ bore our sins.
He died for the ungodly.
He rose again.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith can be forgiven and reconciled to God.
Consider Isaiah 53:5:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.” (KJV)
This is the Gospel.
Not that God became less holy so we could become more comfortable.
But that Jesus Christ accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
And perhaps that is why the consuming fire should awaken something deeper than fear alone.
It should awaken reverence.
Gratitude.
Repentance.
Worship.
A holy astonishment that the God we could never approach on the basis of our own righteousness has invited us to draw near through His Son.
But there is another side to this truth.
And it is one we cannot afford to ignore.
The fire that reveals God's holiness also exposes the danger of treating His grace with contempt.
Hebrews was written to people facing pressure, suffering, and the temptation to turn away from Christ.
Its warnings are serious because abandoning the Son is serious.
Hebrews 12:25 declares:
“See that ye refuse not him that speaketh.” (KJV)
That is the immediate context of the consuming fire.
Do not refuse the One who speaks.
Do not dismiss His warning.
Do not treat His covenant as something ordinary.
Do not exchange the eternal kingdom for temporary security.
And this is where the passage begins to reach into our everyday lives.
Because most people do not wake up one morning and announce, “Today I will abandon everything I believe.”
Sometimes drifting begins quietly.
A prayer life slowly disappears.
The Bible remains closed.
Conviction becomes easier to silence.
A secret sin becomes familiar.
Worship becomes performance.
The heart grows cold while the outward appearance remains religious.
You still know the songs.
You still recognize the verses.
You still know how to say “God is good.”
But somewhere inside, the tenderness you once had toward His Word has begun to fade.
And perhaps nobody knows.
Your family may not notice.
Your church friends may not notice.
Your social media followers may see nothing unusual.
But God sees.
Not because He is searching for an excuse to destroy you.
Because nothing is hidden from His sight.
Hebrews 4:13 reminds us that all things are exposed before the One to whom we must give account.
That truth should sober us.
But it should also lead us to the next verses, where Jesus is presented as our great High Priest and believers are invited to approach the throne of grace for mercy and help.
Do you see the beauty?
The Bible does not expose our need in order to leave us hopeless.
It reveals our need and directs us to Christ.
And maybe that is exactly what you need today.
Not another religious performance.
Not another promise to become a better person through sheer willpower.
Not another carefully edited version of your spiritual life.
Maybe you need to come before Jesus and finally tell the truth.
“Lord, I have been drifting.”
“Lord, I have been hiding.”
“Lord, I know what Your Word says, but I have been making excuses.”
“Lord, I have been carrying bitterness that I refuse to release.”
“Lord, I have looked faithful on the outside while growing cold on the inside.”
“Lord, have mercy on me.”
There is no shame in coming to Christ with genuine repentance.
There is danger in refusing to come.
Because the God who calls us to holiness is also the God who promises mercy to those who turn to Him.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
Notice the words.
Faithful.
Just.
Forgive.
Cleanse.
Not merely tolerate.
Not merely ignore.
Cleanse.
And that brings us to a beautiful biblical picture that is often misunderstood.
Fire in Scripture is not used in only one way.
Sometimes it represents judgment.
Sometimes it accompanies God's presence.
Sometimes it is associated with testing, purification, or refining.
Malachi 3:2–3 describes the Lord using the imagery of a refiner's fire and a purifier of silver.
First Peter 1:6–7 compares the testing of genuine faith through trials with gold refined by fire.
These passages do not mean every painful experience is a direct punishment from God.
Nor do they mean Hebrews 12:29 is secretly promising that God will burn away every problem in our lives.
We must respect the context of each passage.
But together they remind us that God's holiness is never something to trivialize, and that He can use trials to deepen the faith of His people.
And perhaps you have experienced something like that.
You prayed for comfort, and instead discovered how deeply you had depended on things that could never sustain you.
You prayed for spiritual growth, and found yourself confronting pride you had never noticed.
You prayed for a stronger marriage, and realized you needed to repent of words you had been excusing for years.
You prayed to become more like Jesus, and discovered that following Him meant surrendering habits you had grown comfortable defending.
It hurt.
Not every hardship was something you deserved.
Not every loss was a lesson sent specifically to correct you.
And no one should tell a suffering person that every tragedy is God burning away their sin.
Scripture does not authorize that cruel simplification.
But even in suffering, the Lord can sustain, teach, and transform His children.
And when His Word exposes sin, His purpose is not to make repentance impossible.
It is to call us away from destruction and toward life.
That distinction matters.
Because some people have spent years afraid of God in ways that have driven them away from Him rather than toward Him.
Perhaps you grew up hearing about divine judgment but rarely heard about the compassion of Jesus.
Perhaps every mistake made you wonder whether God was waiting to abandon you.
Perhaps you have confused reverence with constant terror.
Listen carefully.
The fear of the Lord is not the same as believing that Jesus is unwilling to receive a repentant sinner.
Jesus said in John 6:37:
“And him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” (KJV)
That is a promise worth holding onto.
The Savior who warns us against sin is the same Savior who receives those who come to Him.
He did not die and rise again so that repentant sinners would spend their lives wondering whether His mercy was real.
He came to save.
He came to reconcile.
He came to redeem.
And He is worthy of our trust.
This is why Hebrews 12:28 is so important.
Immediately before declaring that God is a consuming fire, the writer says:
There it is.
The response to God's holiness is not hopelessness.
It is grateful worship.
We are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken.
A kingdom that does not collapse when economies fail.
A kingdom that does not disappear when governments change.
A kingdom that cannot be destroyed by death.
A kingdom established through the reign of Jesus Christ.
And because we have received such grace, we are called to worship God with reverence and awe.
Not because we are trying to purchase salvation.
Not because we are attempting to earn His acceptance.
But because the God who saves us is worthy of everything we are.
The order matters.
Grace comes first.
Grateful worship follows.
We do not obey in order to make the cross sufficient.
We obey because Christ is Lord, and His grace transforms those who belong to Him.
And this raises a difficult question.
If God's kingdom cannot be shaken, why do we keep building our lives around things that can?
We build our identities around approval.
Then one person's rejection devastates us.
We build our peace around money.
Then one unexpected expense steals our sleep.
We build our worth around appearance.
Then aging begins to frighten us.
We build our security around relationships.
Then disappointment makes us question whether we matter.
We build our happiness around circumstances.
Then suffering arrives, and everything seems to fall apart.
None of these earthly blessings is automatically evil.
But none of them can carry the weight of being our god.
Only Christ can be our ultimate foundation.
And perhaps the consuming fire of Hebrews is confronting something many of us would rather avoid.
We do not merely need God to improve the lives we have constructed.
We need Him to become the center of our lives.
Not one priority among many.
Not an emergency contact.
Not a Sunday appointment.
Our Lord.
Our Redeemer.
Our highest treasure.
Because when everything that can be shaken begins to shake, the only lasting security is the kingdom that cannot be moved.
And the King of that kingdom still bears the scars of the cross.
Think about that.
The risen Jesus is not a distant religious idea.
He is the crucified and resurrected Savior.
The One who defeated death.
The One who intercedes for His people.
The One who calls the weary to come to Him.
The One who will return to judge the living and the dead.
He is full of grace and truth.
And He is worthy of reverence.
You cannot understand the consuming fire correctly by ignoring the cross.
And you cannot understand the cross correctly by ignoring God's holiness.
Separate them, and the Gospel becomes distorted.
Remove holiness, and grace becomes permission to continue in rebellion.
Remove grace, and holiness becomes a message of despair for sinners who cannot save themselves.
But hold them together, and you begin to see the wonder of redemption.
A holy God.
A guilty humanity.
A perfect Savior.
A sufficient sacrifice.
An empty tomb.
A kingdom that cannot be shaken.
And an invitation to repent and believe.
That is why the Gospel is not simply advice about becoming a better person.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ has accomplished salvation for sinners.
And His grace does not leave us unchanged.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God trains believers to reject ungodliness and live godly lives.
True grace does not encourage us to make peace with the sins that nailed our Savior to the cross.
It teaches us to turn away from them.
Not perfectly in our own strength.
But sincerely, continually, through the power of God.
And maybe this is where the message becomes personal.
Because you know the place where conviction has been knocking.
You know the apology you have delayed.
The forgiveness you have resisted.
The secret you have been protecting.
The compromise you keep explaining away.
The truth you keep postponing.
You may have convinced everyone around you that nothing is wrong.
But you know.
And God knows.
So what will you do with His Word?
Will you silence it again?
Will you promise to deal with it another day?
Will you wait until the consequences become unbearable?
Or will you come to Jesus now?
Not because you have already made yourself clean.
But because He is the Savior who cleanses.
Not because your repentance earns forgiveness.
But because His mercy calls you to turn from sin and trust Him.
Not because you can rewrite your past.
But because Jesus Christ can redeem people whose past seemed beyond repair.
That is the heart of our message at Gospel Warrior.
Think of Peter.
He promised loyalty.
Then denied knowing Jesus.
Not once.
Three times.
The rooster crowed.
And Peter wept bitterly.
What must that moment have felt like?
The shame.
The memory of his confident promises.
The unbearable knowledge that he had denied the very Lord he loved.
If the story had ended there, Peter's failure would have defined his final chapter.
But Jesus rose from the dead.
And in John 21, the risen Christ restored Peter to service, calling him again to love and follow Him.
Peter's denial was real.
His tears were real.
His need for restoration was real.
And the grace of Jesus was real.
That is not a story about sin being unimportant.
It is a story about a Savior whose mercy is greater than the failure of a repentant disciple.
Or consider Saul of Tarsus.
A persecutor of the church.
A man whose zeal was terribly misdirected.
A man who approved of Stephen's death and sought to imprison followers of Jesus.
Yet the risen Christ confronted him.
And the persecutor became a servant of the Gospel.
Paul never needed to pretend his past was innocent.
He openly acknowledged what he had been.
But he also testified to the mercy he had received.
In 1 Timothy 1:15, he wrote:
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.” (KJV)
That is the scandal of grace.
Not that God declares evil good.
Not that consequences always disappear.
Not that every broken relationship is automatically restored.
But that through Jesus Christ, guilty people can receive forgiveness, new life, and a future of faithful obedience.
Your past does not have to be your final identity.
Your worst decision does not have to become your eternal destiny.
Your hidden struggle does not have to remain hidden forever.
There is forgiveness in Christ.
There is power to begin walking in truth.
There is grace for the repentant.
And there is hope for the weary.
But please do not mistake that hope for permission to remain unchanged.
The same Jesus who welcomed sinners also called them to repentance.
The same Jesus who forgave also commanded people to follow Him.
The same Jesus who laid down His life will one day judge the world in righteousness.
His mercy is not an excuse to refuse His lordship.
It is the reason we can surrender without despair.
And maybe you are reading this with tears in your eyes because you have spent so long pretending.
You have encouraged everyone else while quietly falling apart.
You have shared Scripture while struggling to believe that God could still use someone like you.
You have told people to pray while your own prayers have become painfully difficult.
You have smiled in church while carrying guilt that nobody knows about.
And somewhere in the silence, you have wondered:
“Does Jesus still want me?”
Hear His invitation.
Come to Him.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Turn from what needs to be abandoned.
Seek help from trustworthy believers where you need support and accountability.
Make restitution where it is appropriate and possible.
Return to His Word.
Pray even when the words come slowly.
And do not confuse the pain of conviction with the absence of mercy.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” (KJV)
That promise belongs to those who are in Christ.
It is not a declaration that sin has no consequences.
It is the glorious announcement that those united to Jesus by faith are no longer under the condemnation their sins deserve.
The consuming fire has not ceased to be holy.
But the believer has a Savior.
And that changes everything.
So when you hear the words “our God is a consuming fire,” do not reduce them to a frightening slogan.
Hear the whole message of Hebrews.
Do not refuse the God who speaks.
Do not despise the grace He offers.
Do not exchange an unshakable kingdom for the temporary comforts of this world.
Do not mistake religious familiarity for genuine faith.
Draw near to God through Jesus Christ.
Receive His mercy.
Worship with reverence.
And live as someone whose life belongs to the King.
Because the greatest tragedy would not be discovering that God is holy.
The greatest tragedy would be hearing His gracious call and refusing the Savior who alone can reconcile you to Him.
And the greatest joy is not finding a way to escape God's holiness.
It is discovering that through Christ, you can belong to the Holy One forever.
If this message has reached a place in your heart you have been avoiding, I want to invite you to respond with something real.
Not a performance.
Not a religious slogan.
An honest response before God.
Someone reading silently may need to hear that repentance is possible, forgiveness is real, and God has not finished His work in His people.
Perhaps you know someone who has grown spiritually cold.
Someone who believes their past is too dark.
Someone who thinks following Jesus means living in constant fear.
Someone who has forgotten the wonder of the Gospel.
Return to Hebrews 12:18–29 when your faith feels distracted, when the world seems unstable, or when you need to remember that God's kingdom cannot be shaken.
And if you have not yet followed Gospel Warrior, I invite you to join us.
Bring your family.
Invite your friends.
Welcome the struggling believer, the curious seeker, the Christian who feels spiritually exhausted, and the person who has not yet understood the good news of Jesus Christ.
We want this community to be a place where Scripture is taken seriously, repentance is never replaced with empty motivation, and the mercy of Christ is proclaimed without compromise.
Because we are not here to build a following around a personality.
We are here to point people to Jesus.
Not out of guilt.
Not because supporting a particular ministry is a requirement for salvation or a measure of how much you love the Lord.
But because freely chosen generosity can become a meaningful expression of gratitude to God and love for others.
Scripture tells us in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that giving should not be done reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
And in Philippians 4:15–18, Paul describes the financial support of Gospel ministry as a gift pleasing to God.
That is the biblical foundation for inviting you to partner with this work.
It is not a substitute for your responsibilities to your local church, and it is not automatically the same thing as the biblical tithe.
But it can be a sincere act of Christian generosity.
An offering made with a willing heart.
A practical way to help more people encounter Scripture, hear the Gospel, and receive encouragement toward faithful discipleship.
And we want you to receive something valuable in return, not merely as a transaction, but as part of our commitment to spiritual growth.

These resources are intended to help believers grow deeper in their understanding of Scripture, strengthen their prayer lives, develop biblical discernment, and become more firmly rooted in Jesus Christ.
These are simply ways to express appreciation for those who choose to stand with the ministry.
It is the opportunity to participate in work that seeks to make Christ known.
A person may read a Scripture reflection during a sleepless night.
A discouraged believer may discover a devotional that reminds them to pray again.
A struggling Christian may be challenged to seek repentance and accountability.
A seeker may encounter a clear explanation of the Gospel for the first time.
We cannot promise what every reader will do.
Only God knows the heart, and only God gives spiritual growth.
But we can faithfully proclaim His Word, serve people with the resources entrusted to us, and trust Him with the results.
And that is a mission worth supporting.
The Gospel is not for sale.
God's grace cannot be purchased.
And no earthly ministry owns the doorway to His kingdom.
Jesus Christ alone is the Savior.
Our responsibility is to point people faithfully toward Him.
That Jesus Christ would be glorified.
That His Word would be understood.
That sinners would repent and believe.
That wounded believers would find biblical encouragement.
That the church would grow in holiness, humility, truth, and love.
And that every testimony of restoration would lead back to the One who makes redemption possible.
Before you leave, I want you to think about one final picture.
Mount Sinai is trembling.
Smoke is rising.
The people are afraid.
The presence of God is overwhelming.
Now look toward Calvary.
There stands Jesus Christ.
The sinless Son of God.
Crucified for sinners.
Bearing the cost of redemption.
And beyond the cross is an empty tomb.
The Savior is risen.
The kingdom is unshakable.
And the invitation of the Gospel still stands.
Repent.
Believe.
Draw near through Christ.
Worship the Lord with reverence and awe.
Do not run from the truth that God is holy.
Run to the Savior who makes reconciliation with the Holy One possible.
Because one day, the applause of this world will be silent.
The possessions we fought to accumulate will belong to someone else.
The titles we chased will lose their importance.
The approval we begged for will no longer matter.
And what will matter eternally is whether we belong to Jesus Christ.
So ask yourself tonight:
Am I merely familiar with the name of Jesus, or have I truly entrusted my life to Him?
Am I grateful for His forgiveness while resisting His authority?
Am I building my life on what can be shaken, or on the kingdom that cannot be moved?
And if the Holy Spirit is using Scripture to expose something in your heart, will you respond with humble repentance rather than another excuse?
You do not need to manufacture an emotional experience.
You need the truth.
You need the Savior.
You need the grace that forgives and transforms.
And you need to remember that the God who calls His people to reverent worship is worthy of far more than occasional attention.
He is worthy of your whole life.
The fire of God's holiness is not extinguished by His grace; through the cross of Jesus Christ, grace opens the way for forgiven sinners to draw near to the Holy One.
